ruleIntents.intent: Checks that each semantic heading's accessible name actually describes the topic/purpose of the content that immediately follows it. It is a semantic relevance judgment: take the heading's accessible-name text, look at the FIRST non-decorative perceivable content after the heading in flat-tree order, and decide whether the heading is an apt description of that content. E.g. heading "Opening Hours" over a paragraph about opening times = descriptive (pass); heading "Weather" over the same opening-hours paragraph = not descriptive (fail). It is NOT checking heading presence, hierarchy/level correctness, uniqueness, or markup validity.
ruleIntents.scLimb: SC 2.4.6 has two limbs: "Headings and labels describe topic or purpose." This rule exercises ONLY the HEADINGS limb (the "describe topic or purpose" requirement as applied to headings). It does not touch the LABELS limb (form-control/label descriptiveness) at all. Within the headings limb it specifically tests the DESCRIPTIVENESS/relevance of the heading text relative to its following content — not whether headings exist (that is 2.4.6 + 1.3.1) and explicitly not whether a visible heading is exposed to AT (that is carved out as 1.3.1, per the Background note).
ruleIntents.applicability: Applies to any semantic heading element that is (a) included in the accessibility tree AND (b) has a non-empty accessible name. "Semantic heading" = native h1-h6 OR any element with role="heading" (e.g. span/p with role=heading + aria-level). Excluded by applicability: pages with no heading (inapplicable 1), headings removed from the a11y tree via hidden (inapplicable 2), and headings whose accessible name is empty string — whether an empty native h1 (inapplicable 3) or role=heading with no text (inapplicable 4). Note an off-screen-but-AT-exposed heading IS still applicable (positioning does not remove it from the tree).
ruleIntents.expectation: Each target heading describes the topic or purpose of the first perceivable, non-decorative content following it, where element order is the flat tree. Pass = the heading's accessible name is an apt description of that next content block (single characters or a single word can suffice — "A" over a glossary list passes). Fail = the name does not describe that next content ("Weather" over an opening-hours paragraph). Only the FIRST following perceivable content is judged; later siblings (a second p) are ignored. The accessible name may come from text, from alt text of a child img, or from a role=heading element. Outcome mapping: any fail = SC not satisfied; all pass or inapplicable = needs further testing (this rule alone cannot confirm 2.4.6 conformance).

ruleIntents.intent: Checks that the programmatic LABEL of a form field describes the field's purpose. Concretely: it locates programmatic labels (HTML `label` elements, and elements referenced via `aria-labelledby`) attached to a form-field control, requires both the control and the label to be visible, and then asks a human-judgment question — does the label text, together with its surrounding visible visual context (nearby headings, sibling label fragments), make the field's purpose clear? "First name:", "Date of birth:" pass; "Menu", "Info:" fail because they are real words but don't describe what the field is for. Crucially it is NOT a presence/accessible-name check (4.1.2) — a field can have a perfectly good accessible name and still FAIL this rule if the label text is non-descriptive. The "descriptive vs not" judgment is the load-bearing part and is inherently semantic.
ruleIntents.scLimb: The "Labels" limb of SC 2.4.6, and within it specifically "Labels ... describe topic or purpose." It does NOT touch the "Headings" limb of the SC at all (headings appear only as visual context that disambiguates otherwise-duplicate labels). It also deliberately carves OUT the adjacent concerns: label PRESENCE/programmatic association is 1.3.1/3.3.2; label-in-accessible-name is 2.5.3; hidden-from-AT is 4.1.2 — the rule maps only the descriptiveness of the visible programmatic label.
ruleIntents.applicability:

A "programmatic label" is narrowed to actual HTML `label` elements OR elements referenced by `aria-labelledby` (not generic WCAG-sense labels). Both the control AND the label must be visible. aspects.title: Headings and labels that are present and topically true but too generic/boilerplate to orient (Information, Section 2, Value, Details)
aspects.description: The hardest real-world 2.4.6 calls are headings and labels that are not WRONG but are uselessly generic and therefore non-orienting: section headings like 'Information', 'More', 'Details', 'Section 2', 'Content', 'Misc', or field labels like 'Field', 'Input', 'Value', 'Setting 1'. Each one technically relates to the content beneath/within it, so a naive topic-match passes, yet it defeats the Understanding intent that a user can 'find the information they seek more easily' and 'predict what each section contains'. A heading 'Information' over a refund-policy section is true-but-not-descriptive; a label 'Value' over an email input is true-but-not-descriptive. This is a graded human judgment (two reviewers can disagree on where 'generic' tips into 'inadequate') that no checker has a semantic notion of. It is the borderline tier the entire ACT corpus deliberately omits.
aspects.scLimb: Both limbs — 'Headings and labels describe topic or purpose.' Covers the descriptiveness/adequacy of heading text (b49b2e limb) AND of form-control/button labels (cc0f0a limb) when the text is technically relevant but too generic to be descriptive.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT fails are deliberate absurd mismatches ('Weather' over opening hours, 'Menu' over a name field) — a 100% topic mismatch. The corpus has NO 'technically-relevant-but-vague' case; the SC's own coverage summary admits there are 'no SUBTLE/borderline cases (e.g. a heading that is vague, overly generic like Information, technically-true-but-unhelpful, or only partially relevant) which is where real-world 2.4.6 judgment is hard.' Generic-ness is exactly the graded judgment the binary pass/fail fixtures hide, and a fully-automated checker cannot judge whether a real word is 'too generic to orient'.

references.quote: When headings are clear and descriptive, users can find the information they seek more easily, and they can understand the relationships between different parts of the content more easily.
These people benefit when section titles make it possible to predict what each section contains.
Authors may also want to consider putting the most important information at the beginning of each heading. This helps users "skim" the headings to locate the specific content they need
Each visual form label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know what input data is expected

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages with REAL, dictionary-valid heading/label text that is genuinely related to its content but too generic to predict what it contains. Each generic page should pair with a 'descriptive' control variant so the judge can see the orienting difference. Keep the content substantive and distinct so the failure is purely the vagueness of the label, not a topic mismatch (which ACT already covers). Mix heading-only pages and form-label-only pages so both limbs are exercised.
suggestedScenarios: A support page whose sections are all headed 'Information', 'More Information', 'Additional Information' over distinct topics (refund policy, shipping, warranty) — topically true but giving no predictive cue about which holds what.

A settings form where every field is labeled 'Value', 'Setting 1', 'Setting 2' over inputs that actually control notification frequency, theme, and language — present labels that fail to convey what each setting does.
An article whose h2 headings read 'Section 1', 'Section 2', 'Section 3' over substantively distinct passages — placeholder headings that survived to production.
A FAQ page whose single heading is 'Details' above a block mixing shipping, returns, and warranty content — true but non-orienting.
A dashboard card headed 'Stuff' over a chart of monthly revenue — generic to the point of useless yet not an outright mismatch.

Pass control: the same support page re-headed 'Refund policy', 'Shipping times', 'Warranty coverage' and the same settings form re-labeled 'Email notifications', 'Color theme', 'Interface language' to contrast skim-ability.

aspects.title: Repeated or near-identical headings/labels among siblings that fail to differentiate sections (relational/uniqueness facet of G130)
aspects.description: G130 states descriptive headings identify sections 'in relation both to the web page as a whole and to other sections of the same web page', so descriptiveness is partly RELATIONAL: a heading or label can describe its own content yet fail to distinguish it from a sibling, defeating heading-to-heading and skim navigation. Real failures: three accordion panels all headed 'Description'; multiple product cards each headed 'Product'; two form fieldsets both holding inputs labeled 'Name' with no Shipping/Billing qualifier on the field; tabs all labeled 'Details'. Each heading/label is individually plausible but collectively non-orienting — a screen-reader user jumping heading-to-heading or scanning a generated heading list hears 'Description, Description, Description'. This is a cross-element, whole-page semantic judgment, not a per-element topic match.
aspects.scLimb: Both limbs — applies G130's relational requirement to heading text and to form-control labels. A heading or label fails not on its own content match but because it is indistinguishable from its siblings.
aspects.whyUncovered: All b49b2e fixtures are single-heading micro-pages (the coverage summary: 'no multiple headings on a page, so heading-to-section scoping and competing next content situations are never exercised'). The only multi-field ACT fixture (b0b11b83, verified: a Shipping fieldset and a Billing fieldset each with 'Name'/'Street') is a PASS where the section heading disambiguates the repeated labels — there is NO fixture where repeated identical headings/labels are left ambiguous. The relational uniqueness facet of G130 is never failed, and an automated checker cannot judge whether sibling sections are confusable.

references.quote: Descriptive headings identify sections of the content in relation both to the web page as a whole and to other sections of the same web page.
Note that the level 2 headings have the distinguishing information at the beginning (i.e., instead of "Preparation for floods", "Preparation for fires", etc).

helps people who use screen readers by ensuring that labels and headings are clearer when presented in a different format — for example, in an automatically generated list of headings, a table of contents, or when jumping from heading to heading within a page.
they can understand the relationships between different parts of the content more easily.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build multi-section / multi-control pages where each heading or label, read alone, looks acceptable, but the SET is undifferentiated. Force the reviewer to imagine the generated heading list or jump-navigation. Include a PASS control identical in structure but with distinguishing text at the start of each heading/label (per the G130 floods/fires example). This is distinct from the generic aspect: here the words may be specific to one panel's content but are reused identically across siblings.
suggestedScenarios: Four FAQ accordions each with the heading 'Question' over different distinct questions — individually plausible, collectively useless when listed by a screen reader.

A two-section form where a Shipping group and a Billing group each contain inputs labeled only 'Name' and 'Street' with NO section heading or per-field qualifier, so a label list reads Name, Street, Name, Street.
A product grid where every card is headed 'Product' with the actual product name only in body text — the heading list gives no differentiation.
An article with three h2 headings all reading 'Overview' introducing the overview of three different chapters.
A tabbed interface whose tab labels (acting as section labels) all read 'Details' over distinct panels of specifications, reviews, and shipping.
Pass control: the same FAQ re-headed with the actual question text, and the same form with 'Shipping name'/'Billing name' qualifiers, so each heading/label list orients correctly.

aspects.title: Graphical/icon-only labels whose glyph is misleading or context-dependent for the control's real function
aspects.description: The Understanding text devotes three paragraphs to icon labels: an image can BE a descriptive label, but 'the same image can be interpreted differently in different contexts' — a magnifying-glass icon next to a text field reads as 'Search', the same icon on a picture reads as 'zoom/magnify'. 2.4.6's label limb and TT 5.B ('The label or instruction can be graphical or textual') therefore require a human visual judgment: is THIS glyph, in THIS placement, a commonly-understood cue for the control's actual function? Failures are present-but-misleading icons: a floppy-disk icon labeling a 'Send' button; a magnifying glass on a button that actually filters rather than searches; a funnel glyph on a control accessibly named 'Search'; a gear icon used as the label for a 'Log out' control; or an icon whose accessible name names the GLYPH ('magnifier') rather than the FUNCTION ('Search'). A checker can confirm an accessible name exists; it cannot judge whether the chosen glyph is the commonly-understood cue for the function in that spot.
aspects.scLimb: Labels limb — the descriptiveness of a control's label when the label is graphical (icon) rather than textual. TT 5.B explicitly admits graphical labels into this limb.
aspects.whyUncovered: No cc0f0a fixture uses a graphical label at all — every label is literal text ('First name:', 'Menu', 'Info:'). The icon-as-label scenario, despite being the single most-elaborated example in the Understanding doc (the entire loupe/magnifier discussion), has ZERO fixtures. Context-dependence (same icon, two meanings) and glyph/function disagreement are inherently semantic+visual judgments the rule never instantiates, and an automated tool that only checks for a non-empty accessible name will pass every one of these.

references.quote: Note that the same image can be interpreted differently in different contexts. However, it can still be considered descriptive if its use is commonly understood in each context.
when accompanying a text field, a loupe or magnifying glass icon with text alternative of "Search" is commonly interpreted as indicating the field is for entering and submitting a search query.
Placed on or near another image, a loupe or magnifying glass icon is commonly interpreted as a means to view a magnified version of the image
The label or instruction can be graphical or textual.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build controls whose only label is an icon (inline SVG or a styled glyph) and where the glyph either contradicts the control's true function or is reused with different effects in different spots on one page. Give each a present accessible name so axe passes, then make the visual glyph the failing element. Include the canonical correct reuse (magnifier=Search next to a query field; magnifier=Zoom on a photo) as the pass control, so the judge contrasts appropriate context-reuse with misuse.
suggestedScenarios: A toolbar where a magnifying-glass icon button (accessible name 'Search') actually triggers a print/zoom preview, not a search — glyph present but mislabels its real function.
A floppy-disk icon button with accessible name 'Submit form' — the universally-read 'save' glyph attached to a send action.
A search field whose trailing icon button uses a funnel/filter glyph but is accessibly named 'Search' — glyph and function disagree.
A gear icon used as the label for a 'Log out' control (gear commonly means settings), with accessible name 'gear'.
Two identical heart-icon buttons on one page: one adds to favorites, one posts a public 'like'; both labeled just 'heart' so the icon fails to disambiguate purpose.
Pass control: a magnifying-glass button next to a query field accessibly named 'Search', and the SAME glyph on a product photo accessibly named 'Zoom image' — correct context-appropriate reuse.

aspects.title: Labels that name the field's topic but omit required data-format / data-requirement cues (format, required, data type)
aspects.description: 2.4.6's label limb is not satisfied merely by a label that names the field's topic; per TT 5.B and G131 the label must make the field's purpose AND its applicable data requirements clear. A label like 'Date of birth:' on a native date picker is the ACT canonical pass, but real failures are subtler: a free-text field labeled only 'Date' that silently demands MM/DD/YYYY; an 'Amount' field that secretly rejects a currency symbol; a 'Card number' field that only accepts un-spaced digits; a required field whose label gives no required indicator while siblings do. The label is present, grammatically describes the topic, and passes axe — yet a user cannot tell what input is expected, which is exactly the descriptiveness shortfall TT 5.B calls out (and an error-after-submit message is explicitly insufficient).
aspects.scLimb: Labels limb — descriptiveness of a form-control label, specifically the 'applicable data requirements' dimension (format, required-status, data type) that the ACT cc0f0a expectation reduces away to a pure topic-match.

No fixture has a field with a non-obvious data format, a required field, or a constrained data type, or a label that is topically right but requirement-blind. The data-requirement dimension that TT 5.B explicitly enumerates is entirely absent, and a checker that only verifies a label is associated and non-empty cannot judge whether the expected format is communicated.

references.quote: Determine whether labels and/or instructions for form components sufficiently describe the purpose and applicable data requirements (date formats, required fields, data type, etc.).
An error message is not sufficient to communicate the expected format to pass this test.
The label may also be used to include text or a text symbol indicating that input is required.
Descriptive labels help users identify specific components within the content.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build forms where each label is a real, topically-correct noun ('Date', 'Amount', 'Card number', 'Password') on a plain text input whose backend imposes a non-obvious format or requirement that the label never states. Make the constraint discoverable only on error (to exercise the TT 'error message not sufficient' note). Pair with a pass control where the same field carries the format/requirement cue inline in the label. Keep the topic correct so the failure is purely the missing requirement cue, not a mismatch (which ACT covers).
suggestedScenarios: A text input (not type=date) labeled only 'Date' whose handler silently requires DD-MM-YYYY, with the format revealed only after a failed submit.
A form with three required fields where two are marked '(required)' but a third required field labeled only 'Email' has no required indicator, so its label fails to convey it must be completed.
A 'Card number' field that only accepts 16 digits with no spaces, labeled merely 'Card number' with no statement of the accepted format.

A 'Password' creation field labeled only 'Password' on a page where complexity rules (12 chars, a symbol) exist but surface only after a rejected submit — error-as-format, which TT says is insufficient.
An 'Amount' currency field labeled 'Amount' that rejects a leading $ sign, with no statement that the symbol must be omitted.
Pass control: the same date field labeled 'Date of birth (MM/DD/YYYY)' and the same required email field labeled 'Email (required)', demonstrating the requirement cue present.

aspects.title: Button/control labels (text) that do not make the control's function clear — generic, ambiguous, or mismatched action verbs
aspects.description: TT 5.B has a second explicit prong: 'Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function', and G131's whole objective is that 'the label for any interactive component makes the component's purpose clear.' A textual button label can be present and grammatical yet fail to convey the action: a row of 'Submit'/'OK'/'Go' buttons that each do different things; a 'Continue' button that actually deletes a draft; multiple 'Edit' / 'Remove' buttons in a list where the label alone does not say WHAT is edited/removed; a primary button labeled 'Click here'. This is a function-descriptiveness judgment over interactive controls, distinct from the topic-descriptiveness of input field labels and distinct from icon labels — it is the button-label half of the labels limb, judged on its action verb and specificity.
aspects.scLimb: Labels limb — specifically the button/control 'function' prong of TT 5.B (parallel to the input 'expected data' prong), applied to text-labeled actionable controls.
aspects.whyUncovered: The cc0f0a corpus tests only single bare INPUT fields with topic-noun labels; it contains no button/control whose label must convey an ACTION, and no case where a generic or mismatched verb leaves the function unclear. TT 5.B's button-function prong is therefore never exercised, and an automated checker that confirms a button has a non-empty accessible name cannot judge whether 'Submit'/'Continue'/'Click here' actually tells the user what the control does in context.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages with text-labeled buttons/controls (not inputs, not icons) whose label is present but fails the function test: generic verbs, mismatched verbs, or labels that do not say what object they act on in a repeated list. Each button must be plausibly correct in isolation. Include a pass control where each button's label names its specific action ('Save profile', 'Delete this comment'). Keep this separate from the icon aspect (visual glyph) and the input aspect (expected data).
suggestedScenarios: A dialog with three buttons all labeled 'OK' that respectively save, discard, and export — the label fails to distinguish the functions.
A multi-step wizard whose primary button reads 'Continue' but actually submits and charges the user's card with no further confirmation.
A list of five saved drafts where each row's only action button reads 'Remove' with no indication of WHICH draft it removes (label gives no object).
A primary call-to-action button reading 'Click here' on a page about downloading a tax form — present label, no function cue.
A toolbar of three text buttons labeled 'Go', 'Go', 'Go' that run a search, clear the form, and open settings respectively.
Pass control: the same dialog re-labeled 'Save changes', 'Discard changes', 'Export PDF', and the draft list re-labeled 'Delete "Q3 report" draft', so each function is clear.

aspects.title: Heading/label descriptiveness that holds in source order but breaks under visual reading order, or for collapsed/dynamic content
aspects.description: The b49b2e rule's own Assumptions name two hard cases it never instantiates: (a) divergence between flat-tree order and visual reading order via CSS positioning/grid/flex order, and (b) headings for expandable/collapsed (hidden) content. A heading can be descriptive of the content that follows it in the DOM but sit visually above unrelated content (CSS order reorders columns/cards), so a sighted user sees 'Pricing' over the FAQ block; or a heading describes content that is only correct once a panel is expanded, while the collapsed default exposes a different (mismatched) summary. Judging these requires rendering the page and reading it visually AND interacting with disclosure state — neither of which a static automated checker or a flat-tree-only rule performs. TT pointedly judges the VISIBLE heading-to-content relationship, which is exactly what diverges here.
aspects.scLimb: Headings limb primarily (descriptiveness of a heading relative to the content a user actually perceives under it), with the labels limb implicated when a control's label changes on interaction. Tests the rendered/interacted descriptiveness the flat-tree rule and static checkers miss.
aspects.whyUncovered: The coverage summary states the rule's own hard cases — 'flat-tree vs visual reading order divergence via CSS positioning/grid/flex order, and headings for expandable/collapsed (hidden) content — are called out in the Assumptions but have NO test fixtures here.' Every b49b2e fixture is heading-then-single-paragraph in trivial DOM order. A static checker reads source order, not rendered visual order or post-interaction state, so it cannot detect a heading that is descriptive in the DOM but mis-orienting on screen or after a disclosure toggles. TT explicitly judges the visible heading-to-content relationship and includes interaction-driven label changes.

references.quote: For each visually identified heading, compare the heading text to the content beneath the heading.
Any changes to form labels that occur automatically or as a result of interaction should be included.
When headings are clear and descriptive, users can find the information they seek more easily, and they can understand the relationships between different parts of the content more easily.
Descriptive headings help users find specific content and orient themselves within the web page.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Use self-contained HTML+CSS (and minimal inline JS for disclosure) to create a deliberate divergence between source order and what the user perceives. For layout cases, use CSS grid-template-areas / flex order / position to move a heading visually over content it does not describe while keeping it DOM-adjacent to matching content. For state cases, use a details/summary or aria-expanded toggle where the heading is apt for the expanded body but the collapsed default summary mismatches, or where an interaction relabels a control to something non-descriptive. Pair each with a pass control where rendered order and state keep the heading apt.
suggestedScenarios: A two-column CSS-grid layout where 'Shipping options' is DOM-adjacent to the shipping list but CSS grid-area places it visually directly above the unrelated 'Customer reviews' block.
A flexbox row using order: -1 to pull a 'Summary' heading visually in front of the 'Legal disclaimer' card, while in source it precedes the actual summary.
A collapsed details/summary whose summary reads 'Pricing' but, once expanded, the panel body is the return-policy text — the heading is mis-orienting in the default visual state.
An accordion where each panel's heading is descriptive only after expansion; collapsed, the visible trigger text ('More') fails to describe what will appear.
A control labeled 'Show details' that, after click, relabels to 'Submit' (an interaction-driven label change) where the new label no longer describes its function.
Pass control: the same grid/flex page with CSS order matching source so each heading sits visually over the content it describes, and a details/summary whose summary text matches its expanded body.

aspects.title: Visible label/heading and accessible name diverge in descriptiveness — one surface is descriptive, the other is not
aspects.description: 2.4.6 is judged differently by the two methodologies: ACT/b49b2e judges the ACCESSIBLE NAME, while TT 5.B/10.A judge the VISIBLE label/heading. The untested gap is when the visible text and the accessible name DIVERGE in descriptiveness. A field visibly labeled 'First name' but given aria-label='field1' (sighted user fine, screen-reader user stranded); or the reverse, a visibly cryptic 'X' button whose aria-label='Close dialog' is the descriptive one; or a heading visibly reading 'Quarterly Earnings' whose aria-labelledby points at a stray 'Q' so AT announces just 'Q'. The Understanding doc warns 2.4.6 is independent of 4.1.2 — a control 'can have an appropriate accessible name and therefore pass 4.1.2, but still fail this success criterion if the label is inaccurate or insufficiently clear.' Deciding which surface to judge, and whether the divergent name is descriptive, is a human call: the name exists (so 4.1.2 / axe pass) but the two surfaces carry different meanings against the field's true purpose.
aspects.scLimb: Both limbs — applies to form-control labels and to headings whose accessible name is computed from an override (aria-label / aria-labelledby) that differs in descriptiveness from the visible text.
aspects.whyUncovered:
The coverage summary notes accessible-name computation is exercised 'only trivially (literal text, one img alt, one role=heading); no aria-label/aria-labelledby overrides, no name composed from multiple sources, no name that differs from visible text.' The cc0f0a aria-labelledby fixtures keep visible and programmatic text identical — verified: fixture fa5104f9 sets both the visible

and the labelledby source to the same word 'Menu', so there is no descriptiveness DIVERGENCE between eye and AT. A checker confirms a non-empty accessible name (passing 4.1.2) and cannot weigh the visible-vs-announced surfaces against the control's purpose, which is the explicitly-separate 2.4.6 judgment.

references.quote: It is possible for controls and inputs to have an appropriate accessible name (e.g. using aria-label="…") and therefore pass Success Criterion 4.1.2, but to still fail this success criterion (if the label is inaccurate or insufficiently clear or descriptive).
Review the visual labels and/or instructions provided for each form component/control.
For each visually identified heading, compare the heading text to the content beneath the heading.

this success criterion does not take into consideration whether or not alternative methods of providing an accessible name for form controls and inputs have been used — that aspect is covered separately by

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build controls/headings where the visible text and the computed accessible name disagree on descriptiveness. Use aria-label / aria-labelledby (pointing at a stray short element) so the accessible name is well-formed and non-empty (4.1.2 passes) but mismatched in clarity from the visible text. Include BOTH directions (visible-descriptive/announced-vague AND visible-cryptic/announced-descriptive) so the judge must reason about which surface governs. Pair with a pass control where visible and accessible name agree and are both descriptive.
suggestedScenarios: An input visibly associated with a <label>First name</label> but also carrying aria-label='input1', which wins the name computation — visible descriptive, announced name useless.
A button visibly reading 'Delete account' but given aria-label='Submit' — visible clear, programmatic generic, the two surfaces disagree on function.
A heading visibly reading 'Quarterly Earnings' whose accessible name comes from aria-labelledby pointing at a stray 'Q' element, so AT announces just 'Q'.
A search input visibly labeled 'Search products' but given aria-label='text field' — divergent descriptiveness across the two surfaces.
Reverse case: a visibly cryptic toolbar button 'X' whose aria-label='Close dialog' is the descriptive one — tests whether judging visible vs programmatic flips the verdict.
Pass control: a field where the visible label 'Email address' and aria-label='Email address' agree and are both descriptive.

This is the canonical context-appropriate reuse described verbatim in the SC 2.4.6 Understanding doc, so the graphical labels are descriptive and the page passes; included to contrast appropriate reuse against the misuse in case-01..05.
pages.mechanism: Both buttons expose role=button with a non-empty accessible name (loupe SVGs aria-hidden). The first, accompanying a text field and named "Search", is the commonly-understood query affordance; the second, placed on an image and named "Zoom image", is the commonly-understood magnify affordance. In each placement the glyph's conventional meaning matches the context and the name names the function (not the glyph), and each control does what its label says — so both graphical labels are descriptive, satisfying the 2.4.6 label limb.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Automated tools also pass this page (both buttons have non-empty names; verified via accessibility tree showing role=button name="Search" and name="Zoom image") — but here the pass verdict is correct, and that is the point. A tool cannot tell that this is the appropriate reuse the Understanding doc endorses while case-01..05 are inappropriate misuse, because that distinction is a human judgment about whether each glyph's conventional meaning fits its context. The aspect requires a human to ratify good reuse as confidently as flagging bad reuse.

problems: TT 5.B scope wrinkle: the cited Trusted Tester Test 5.B is explicitly a *form-label* test ('Each visual form label...'), and its DNA condition is 'the page has no form elements'. This page has NO <form> and no form controls — only toolbar buttons — so a strict TT-procedure reading would mark 5.B as DNA/inapplicable rather than a literal PASS/FAIL. The 'failed' verdict is correct at the WCAG SC 2.4.6 level (a button's accessible name is a label, and a misleading label fails the SC's descriptiveness requirement; the doc keys its outcome to SC 2.4.6, and TT note line 24 'so users know its function' + line 28 'graphical or textual' do apply), but the case leans on a forms-scoped test for a non-form control. WCAG-quote context caveat (handled correctly but worth noting): the quoted loupe/Search sentence is conditioned on the icon 'accompanying a text field'; the immediately following (unquoted) sentence states a loupe near another image commonly means zoom/magnify. The passage's real point is context-dependence of icon meaning. The page uses this correctly to argue the loupe label is NOT descriptive of a print-preview action, so the citation supports the failure direction.

Borderline SC-attribution debate: a 'Search'-labeled button that opens print preview is arguably also/instead a 4.1.2-style name-vs-behavior mismatch. The genuine barrier is that aria-label="heart" DISCARDS the distinct visible text ('Saved to my cookbook' vs '312 public likes') that a sighted user relies on, leaving the accessible name non-descriptive for both controls. A strict TT 5.B reading judges the VISUAL label — and the visible button text here IS distinct/descriptive, which would read as PASS for sighted users. The real defect is closer to a visible-vs-accessible-name divergence (this corpus has a dedicated 'visible-vs-accessible-name-divergence' group) than a pure graphical-label-context failure.

Selector mismatch with the doc's framing: the .md lists BOTH #saveBtn and #likeBtn as carrying the issue (the ambiguity is relational between the pair), but the element-under-test selector targets only #likeBtn. The failure is only meaningful as a pair — a single button named 'heart' in isolation would be a different (still-arguable) case.

pages.scenario: UK borough council 'Report a missed bin collection' form: a plain text input (not type=date, so no native picker hints at order) labelled only 'Date' whose JS validator silently accepts only day-first DD-MM-YYYY and rejects 11/06/2026, 2026-11-06, '6 November 2026'. The DD-MM-YYYY format is disclosed for the first time only in the post-submit error.
pages.mechanism: Label names the topic ('Date') correctly and is associated + non-empty, but communicates none of the applicable data requirement (day-first DD-MM-YYYY). The format constraint lives only in the submit-handler regex /^(0[1-9]|[12]\d|3[01])-(0[1-9]|1[0-2])-\d{4}$/ and the after-submit error, which TT 5.B's Note says is insufficient. A screen-reader user hears 'Date, edit text' and cannot know the field rejects reasonable inputs.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The <label> is present, associated via for/id, and non-empty, and the input has valid attributes, so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse report a correctly labelled field. No static scanner parses the submit-handler regex to learn the field demands day-first DD-MM-YYYY, and none can judge that 'Date' alone fails to tell a user what format is expected; recognising that the label is topically right but requirement-blind needs human reasoning.

pages.scenario: Nonprofit donation form with a legend 'Fields marked (required) must be completed.' Two fields are labelled 'First name (required)' and 'Gift amount (required)'; a third field that is ALSO required (has the required attribute, blocks submit, receives the receipt) is labelled only 'Email' with no '(required)' word, silently breaking the page's own stated convention.
pages.mechanism: The label 'Email' names the topic correctly and the field carries a real required attribute, but the visible label omits the required-status cue that the page taught the user marks mandatory fields and that sibling labels carry. The descriptiveness shortfall is that the label fails to convey the required data requirement TT 5.B enumerates and G131 says a label may carry.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The label is associated and non-empty and the field has a valid required attribute, so axe-core sees a correctly labelled, required input and may even read 'required' as a positive signal. No checker compares the visible '(required)' convention used on sibling labels against this one to spot the inconsistency, nor judges that given the page's own legend the omission makes the label non-descriptive of its requirement — a contextual human reading.

citation.quote: The label may also be used to include text or a text symbol indicating that input is required.

pages.scenario: E-commerce bike-shop checkout. Sibling fields carry their format inline ('Expiry (MM/YY)', 'Security code (3 digits)') but the card-number field is labelled merely 'Card number'. Its validator is /^\d{16}$/ — it accepts only 16 bare digits and rejects the grouped form '4111 1111 1111 1111' that is printed on the card and that nearly everyone types. No mask, no inline cue; the format appears only in the post-submit error.
pages.mechanism: Label states the topic ('Card number') but not the applicable data type/format (exactly 16 digits, no spaces). The constraint lives only in the /^\d{16}$/ submit handler and the error message. The contrast with sibling labels that DO show their format sharpens the shortfall — the field with the strictest, least-obvious constraint is the one missing its cue.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The label is present, associated, and non-empty and the input has valid attributes (inputmode, autocomplete=cc-number), so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse report a correctly labelled field. No scanner executes or parses the /^\d{16}$/ regex to discover spaces are rejected, and none can judge that 'Card number' alone fails to communicate the accepted format — especially when its own siblings show theirs.

citation.quote: Each visual form label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know what input data is expected

pages.scenario: SaaS workspace signup. The password-creation field is labelled 'Password' with a visible help line that only says 'Choose something memorable' — friendly but misleading. The real complexity rules (at least 12 characters AND at least one symbol) are enforced only by the submit handler and disclosed only in the error after a rejected submit: error-as-format.
pages.mechanism: Neither the label ('Password') nor its associated instruction ('Choose something memorable') communicates the applicable data requirements (>=12 chars, a symbol); the rule lives only in the validator (v.length>=12 && /[^A-Za-z0-9]/.test(v)) and the post-submit error. Presence of a label and an instruction satisfies 3.3.2/4.1.2, but the descriptiveness limb fails because the requirement surfaces only on error — which TT 5.B forbids.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The label is associated and non-empty AND there is a visible instruction paragraph, so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse see a generously labelled field; the presence of some help text can even read as a positive signal. No scanner evaluates whether that instruction states the enforced policy or reads the validator to learn the 12-char/symbol rule. Judging that 'Choose something memorable' fails to convey the real requirement is a semantic comparison only a human can make.

pages.scenario: German statutory health-insurer portal (lang=de) reimbursement claim. The amount field is labelled with the correct topic noun 'Betrag' (Amount). Its validator /^\d+,\d{2}$/ accepts only a comma decimal with exactly two fraction digits and NO currency symbol and NO thousands separator (e.g. '85,00'); the natural German entry '85,00 €' is rejected solely for the euro sign, as are '85.00' and '1.250,00'. A sibling field 'IBAN (DE, 22 Stellen)' DOES carry its format; the required shape for Betrag appears only in the post-submit error.
pages.mechanism: Label 'Betrag' states the topic but omits the locale-specific data requirement: comma decimal, two fraction digits, no € symbol, no thousands dot. A German user typing '85,00 €' as on paper is rejected with no way to anticipate it from the label; the format is disclosed only in the after-submit error. Pure missing-requirement limb, not a topic mismatch.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The label is present, associated, and non-empty in the document's declared language, so axe-core/WAVE/Lighthouse report a properly labelled field. No scanner reads the /^\d+,\d{2}$/ validator to learn the euro symbol and thousands separator are rejected, and none has the locale knowledge to judge that a German amount label should state 'no € symbol, comma decimal' — requiring a human who understands German number conventions.

citation.quote: Determine whether labels and/or instructions for form components sufficiently describe the purpose and applicable data requirements (date formats, required fields, data type, etc.).

pages.scenario: PASS / boundary control: a term-life insurance quote form that reuses the exact failing fields from case-01 (free-text date) and case-02 (required email) but now carries each requirement cue inline: 'Date of birth (MM/DD/YYYY)', 'Email (required)' (consistent with the '*' legend), and 'ZIP code (5 digits)'. The input attributes (placeholder/pattern) agree with the labelled format, so a user knows what input is expected before submitting and no requirement is hidden behind an error.
pages.mechanism: Each label now conveys both topic and applicable data requirement: the date format up front (no error reliance), the required-status consistent with the legend, the ZIP data type/length. The accessible name includes the requirement, so a screen-reader user hears 'Date of birth (MM/DD/YYYY), required, edit text' and can satisfy the field before submission — the canonical-pass shape G131 describes.

The genuine pass/fail difference (requirement cue present vs absent) is exactly the dimension no checker evaluates; confirming this page truly passes the descriptiveness limb requires a human to read the label and judge the format/required cue is present and accurate.

pages.scenario: A SaaS analytics dashboard editor raises an unsaved-changes alertdialog whose three action buttons are ALL labeled 'OK'; they respectively save (persist edits), discard (revert), and export (.json), and are even rendered in a different order than the prose lists them. The visible button label alone never says which 'OK' does which.
pages.mechanism: Three sibling controls perform three distinct consequential functions (save/discard/export) yet share the generic, verb-less accessible name 'OK'. The label conveys only 'this is a confirm button', not WHICH function; the disambiguating prose is present but not associated with any button, and DOM order does not match prose order. A screen-reader user tabbing the dialog hears 'OK, OK, OK' and cannot tell save from discard from export — failing TT 5.B's button-function prong (G131: label must make the component's purpose clear).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every button has a non-empty accessible name ('OK') and valid role, so axe button-name, WAVE, and Lighthouse pass; duplicate accessible names across siblings are not a flagged violation. Judging that 'OK' fails to convey FUNCTION — and that three identical 'OK's on save/discard/export is dangerous — requires reading the dialog prose, mapping it to the buttons, and reasoning about each action's consequence: an irreducible human semantic judgment no static rule models.

pages.scenario: A four-step pet-insurance quote wizard showing 'Review' as step 3 (with 'Done' still ahead) has a primary button labeled 'Continue'. The label implies advancing to the next step, but the control actually BINDS the policy and charges the saved card immediately with no further confirmation; step 4 is only a receipt.
pages.mechanism: Mismatched action verb: a generic progression verb ('Continue'), reinforced by a step indicator that makes the user expect another step, labels a consequential, irreversible commit-and-charge action. The accessible name affirmatively signals navigation, not commitment, so neither sighted nor screen-reader users are warned by the label that activating it spends money. TT 5.B requires the visible button label to make the function clear; here it actively misrepresents the function.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: 'Continue' is a non-empty, conventional, well-formed accessible name that every name/role checker rates as a GOOD label — there is nothing wrong with the string in isolation. The failure lives entirely in the gap between the label's implied action and the click handler's real effect (bind + charge), discoverable only by reading the step indicator and fine print and reasoning that 'Done' is merely a receipt. No automated tool reasons about whether a verb matches what the handler does.

pages.scenario: A municipal transit trip planner has an ARIA toolbar with two stop fields and three text buttons ALL labeled 'Go': the first runs the trip search, the second clears the From/To fields, and the third opens the rider settings panel. pages.mechanism: Generic action verb ('Go') repeated on three controls with three different functions. 'Go' implies execute-the-search, so a screen-reader user moving through the toolbar hears 'Go, Go, Go' and reasonably activates one expecting departures, instead erasing entered stops or being taken to settings. The label conveys neither the differing functions nor any warning of the destructive/navigational ones; for two of the three the verb is outright misleading (fails TT 5.B / G131).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Each button has a non-empty accessible name and valid role inside a labelled toolbar, so button-name, WAVE, and Lighthouse pass; repeated identical names are not flagged. A tool cannot know that one 'Go' searches, one clears, and one opens settings — the functions live in the click handlers and page behaviour, not in any attribute. Recognising that one verb cannot distinguish three functions, and that 'Go' actively misdescribes the clear and settings actions, is a semantic, behavioural reading no static check performs.

This does NOT change the verdict — WCAG SC 2.4.6 itself (the primary, verbatim-verified citation) covers any present label including a standalone button label, so 'failed' holds. But the doc's reliance on the 5.B 'button-function prong' as the mechanism is at the edge of that test's documented scope.

Cosmetic: the inspect tool's tabOrder lists ~12 'Click here' stops; this is the tool cycling Tab on a single-control page (focus wraps back to the same button), not multiple buttons. The AX tree shows exactly one button (backendNodeId 21). Not a page defect.

Minor caveat (not a blocker): all three buttons carry onclick="return false" and have NO functional JS — the three distinct functions (run-search / clear-form / open-settings) exist only in HTML comments and the .md doc, not in executable code. The failure therefore relies on accepting the documented intent as ground truth. This is the consistent convention across all 6 sibling cases in this directory (none wire real JS), so it is acceptable, but a strictly code-only reader could argue the buttons all do nothing equally.
aria-live="off" on the results region is unusual phrasing (off is the default; harmless and not under test).

Secondary citation defect (minor): the .md cites refs/wcag-understanding/headings-and-labels.html for 'Labels and headings do not need to be lengthy...' but that file does not exist anywhere under refs/ and the quoted sentence appears nowhere in the corpus (grep returns nothing). It is likely a genuine W3C Understanding-document quote attributed to a file that is not checked into this repo. Non-load-bearing — the primary TT 5.B citation is solid — so it does not change the PASS verdict, but it should be removed or repointed to a real path.

This is a deliberate PASS control, so there is no accessibility error to confirm (errorIsReal=false is correct by design, not a defect). The page would also be passed by automated checkers (all accessible names non-empty), but the .html/.md are explicit and honest about this; the human-judgment value is in the function-descriptiveness (label quality, not presence) dimension that separates it from the failing case-01..05.

Outcome is interpretation-dependent (correctly so, by corpus design): the page PASSES the cited ACT rule b49b2e's own automated procedure (which orders by the flat tree, where the h2 is glued to the shipping text) and FAILS only under the rendered-order TT 10.A judgment. The .md is honest about this, but expected:'failed' is true only under the visible/manual interpretation, not under the named ACT rule itself.

Arguably the rendered mis-orientation (heading over the wrong content due to source-vs-visual divergence) overlaps with SC 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence / 2.4.10; it is still defensible under 2.4.6 because TT 10.A judges the VISIBLE heading-to-content relationship, but the SC boundary is a touch soft.

Outcome is AT-dependent (correctly disclosed in the doc): a screen-reader user walking the flat tree hears each heading glued to its matching content and is NOT affected; the failure manifests ONLY for sighted/low-vision/cognitive users reading the rendered visual column. So per ACT rule b49b2e (which orders strictly by the flat tree) the rule would PASS — the doc rightly frames the 'failed' label as an SC 2.4.6 failure under human visual judgment, NOT a b49b2e auto-failure. This is a correct but nuanced distinction, not a defect.
Minor: the rule's quoted Assumptions sentence contains a typo 'Headings and Label' (singular) which the doc reproduces verbatim — acceptable since it is an exact quote of the source file.

Framing nuance (not a defect): the element under test has AX role DisclosureTriangle, not `heading` (confirmed by inspect.js ax.role and the puppeteer snapshot). So this is the general-sense-heading / 'Labels' reading of SC 2.4.6, not a literal h1-h6 heading. The doc acknowledges this ('the <summary> acts as the section heading'), and b49b2e's own Background confirms content that is not in scope of the rule 'can still fail Success Criterion 2.4.6 Headings and Labels', so it remains within 2.4.6 scope — but a strict reviewer should note the summary is not a `heading` role.

b49b2e cannot, even in principle, FAIL this page (its Applicability requires a semantic heading element AND its Assumptions carve out hidden/expandable content). The doc correctly uses the citation as a scoping/carve-out, not as the failing rule — so the page's 'failed' verdict rests on SC 2.4.6 itself plus TT 10.A, with b49b2e cited only to explain non-detectability. This is honest, but means there is NO ACT rule that programmatically asserts the failure; the keep-value rests entirely on human semantic judgment.

SEVERE METADATA MISMATCH: the prompt's claimed scenario/mechanism/citation/element describe a DIFFERENT page than the file on disk. Prompt claims a 'Higher-ed course FAQ accordion' with generic 'Read article →' triggers (headings limb, G130, selector #t1). The actual case-04.html is a 'Send money — Meridian Bank' 3-step money-transfer WIZARD with a 'Continue' #primary button (labels limb, TT 5.B / G131). The HTML <title> is 'Send money — Meridian Bank' and the only buttons are 'Cancel' and 'Continue'.

ELEMENT UNDER TEST DOES NOT EXIST: prompt selector is #t1, but grep of the HTML finds no id 't1' anywhere; the inspect tool returns the full document tree (no targeted node) for #t1. The element carrying the documented issue is actually #primary. The browser AX tree confirms only two buttons exist: name='Cancel' and name='Continue' (both role=button).

CITATION MISMATCH: prompt cites WCAG G130 ('Determine if the web page contains headings. Check that each heading identifies its section of the content.'). The companion .md cites G131 + Trusted Tester 5.B instead. The G130 quote is irrelevant to this page (no failing heading; the sole <h1> 'Send money' correctly describes the page).

Because the prompt's claimed mechanism (FAQ accordion / hidden descriptive heading / G130 headings limb / #t1) cannot be located on the actual page, the prompt-as-stated is REFUTED: errorIsReal=false and expectedOutcomeCorrect=false against the prompt's framing.

Substantive note (judging the ACTUAL file on its own): the .md's own thesis — 'Continue' under-describes the irreversible 'send' function on step 3 — is a defensible but SOFT 2.4.6 labels failure that leans into 3.2.5 (Change on Request) territory; 'Continue' is arguably descriptive of 'advance the flow', so a reviewer could reasonably call this a pass for 2.4.6. The .md's three citations (TT 5.B button-label line, TT 5.B Notes, G131 Procedure) all verify VERBATIM against refs/trusted-tester/sc-2.4.6-headings-and-labels.md and wcag-techniques/general/G131.html.

The page itself is self-contained (no external resources, no JS errors, ok=true) and non-trivial, so the underlying HTML/MD pair is usable — but the orchestrator must re-pair this file with its correct metadata (wizard/labels/#primary/G131), not the FAQ-accordion/headings packaging supplied in the prompt.
See above

No defect — this is a deliberate PASS-boundary control case, not a failing case, so 'errorIsReal=false' is the INTENDED and correct state (the documented expected outcome is 'passed', and the page genuinely passes).

Citation is sound: the quoted Test 10.A line 'The heading describes the topic or purpose of its content.' appears verbatim at refs/trusted-tester/sc-2.4.6-headings-and-labels.md line 41 ('Evaluate Results (PASS if)'), correctly attributed to TT v5.1.3 Test 10.A. Minor note only: the .md doc's own Citation section also pairs it with a WCAG Understanding 2.4.6 'In brief/Goal' quote which I did not byte-verify against a local WCAG file, but it is supplementary and not the load-bearing mechanism citation.

Minor (non-blocking): the .md claims 'a full axe.run (default ruleset + experimental label-content-name-mismatch) reports 0 violations' but the corroborating inspect tool runs no checker, so this specific 0-violations figure was not independently verified here. Reasoning supports it (the accessible name is non-empty, the label is associated, and label-content-name-mismatch/ACT 2ee8b8 does not apply since there is no visible text node inside the control), so it does not change the verdict — but it is an unverified empirical assertion in the doc.

CITATION SCOPE TENSION (minor, not a hallucination): the quote 'Each visual button label is sufficiently clear and descriptive, so users know its function.' is VERBATIM at refs/trusted-tester/sc-2.4.6-headings-and-labels.md line 24 (TT Test 5.B, Evaluate-Results criterion 2). But 5.B is literally scoped to the VISUAL label ('Review the visual labels...', 'Each VISUAL button label...'). The visible label here is 'Delete account', which IS adequate/accurate for the function, so 5.B read strictly would PASS. The actual defect is in the ACCESSIBLE (announced) name 'Delete account draft', which is more squarely a 2.5.3 Label-in-Name / 4.1.2 accuracy concern. The 'failed' verdict is still defensible under the broad SC 2.4.6 intent (the AT-perceived label misdescribes purpose for SR users), but the cited TT limb maps imperfectly to the mechanism.

The page's own comment/doc claim that 2.5.3 PASSES (visible ⊆ name) is correct for the substring rule, but a careful 2.5.3 human review could also flag that the speech-input target word set diverges; this overlap means the case is not cleanly isolated to 2.4.6 — it is a multi-SC boundary case.

BORDERLINE VERDICT (not a defect, but the most contestable of the four cases): the visible label is '✕', which is arguably the single most conventional 'close' glyph in any toolbar — a competent human Trusted Tester could reasonably mark this PASS, not FAIL. The case picks the conservative TT 5.B visible-label limb and labels it 'failed'; the .md is transparent that a pure accessible-name reading yields 'passed' and that this divergence is the deliberate point. The outcome is defensible but genuinely debatable, so its value as ground truth depends on accepting the conservative reading.

MINOR REAL-WORLD SEVERITY: the control has a correct role and an excellent descriptive accessible name ('Close conversation'); AT/screen-reader/braille users are fully served. The only affected population is sighted users who must infer the bare '✕' — a low-impact, near-universally-understood convention.

Defensible-but-debatable SC framing: the divergence (visible descriptive Arabic label vs. AT-announced non-descriptive Latin slug) is filed as a 2.4.6 failure on the announced-label surface. A reviewer who reads 2.4.6 as operating on the *visible* label could argue 2.4.6 PASSES (the visible label IS descriptive) and that the AT-only defect is more naturally a 4.1.2 / accname concern. The doc pre-empts this by arguing 4.1.2 passes (non-empty name) so only 2.4.6's announced-label descriptiveness fails — a defensible reading, and either way the issue requires human semantic judgment. Not a defect, just a framing nuance worth noting.

TASK-PROMPT MISMATCH (not a page defect): the orchestrator metadata describes a totally different case — a newsletter signup with a 'Search' loupe icon button + email field, claimed outcome 'passed', selector button.iconbtn[aria-label="Search"]. The ACTUAL files (case-06.html/.md) are a museum-gallery HEADING mis-attribution case, claimed outcome 'failed', selector h2#h-roman. There is no <button>, no search/email field, and no aria-label="Search" anywhere in case-06.html. I judged the actual files; the prompt's element/scenario/citation block is stale and does not apply.

CITATION FRAMING IMPRECISION: the .md cites TT 10.A '2.4.6-heading-purpose'. The Test Condition quote 'Each heading describes the topic or purpose of its content.' appears VERBATIM at line 34 of refs/trusted-tester/sc-2.4.6-headings-and-labels.md (citation is genuine). BUT TT 10.A 'How to Test' compares the VISUALLY IDENTIFIED heading text to content beneath it; the VISIBLE text here ('Roman Britain') correctly describes the Roman content, so a literal TT-10.A reading would PASS. The failure exists only on the AT/announced surface (aria-labelledby overrides accName to 'Anglo-Saxon Treasures'). The defect is thus really an announced-name-vs-content divergence (4.1.2-adjacent) presented under 2.4.6; the .md slightly overstates that TT 10.A 'fails' when TT works from visual text.
Secondary citation 'ACT rule b49b2e (Heading is descriptive)' is name-dropped in the .md but no b49b2e file exists under refs/ (grep returned nothing). Not the primary citation, so minor.
